items.quote: “Finally all the trees said to the thornbush, ‘Come and be our king.’
items.contrast: The trees as the prospective subjects versus the nearby gods and humans.
items.reason: Gods and humans are plausible distractors because they are mentioned immediately before, but they are only those cheered by the vine’s wine. “Our” refers to the trees speaking to the thornbush.

items.quote: their illnesses were cured and the evil spirits left them.
items.contrast: The evil spirits departing versus the illnesses being cured.
items.reason: Illnesses are a plausible alternative because both results occur when the handkerchiefs and aprons reach the sick. However, only the evil spirits are said to leave. “Items” is an avoidable generic substitute for the named handkerchiefs and aprons, and “on the items’ arrival” is awkwardly indirect.

items.quote: So the man of God returned with him and ate and drank in his house.
items.contrast: The man of God as the intended eater and drinker versus the old prophet who reports the claim.
items.reason: The old prophet is plausible because he voices the claim and owns the house, but the third-person “him” and “he” refer to the person he is addressing. The following action confirms that this is the man of God.

items.quote: ‘They will surely come out, and then we will take them alive and get into the city.’
items.contrast: Entering the city after taking the people alive versus leaving the camp earlier to set the trap.
items.reason: Leaving the camp is plausible because it is part of the king’s account of the Arameans’ plan, but it occurs before the expected capture. The quoted sequence explicitly places getting into the city after taking the people alive.

items.quote: These four were descendants of Rapha in Gath, and they fell at the hands of David and his men.
items.contrast: David and his men defeating all four descendants versus Jonathan defeating the single giant described in this battle.
items.reason: Jonathan is plausible because he is explicitly named as killing one descendant. The closing sentence broadens the scope to all four and attributes their defeat collectively to David and his men.
